contribution: The chapter brings the electrical measurement of the energy of a photon: the operation of an LED through the energy gap of a semiconductor and the photon, the threshold voltage and the equation $eU_\text{k} \approx hf = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, determining the threshold voltage from a $(U, I)$ graph, the Planck constant from the slope of the graph $(f, U_\text{k})$ with Graphical Analysis Pro, and comparing the spectra of an LED, a laser diode and an incandescent lamp.
learn: explain why the threshold voltage of an LED depends on the wavelength of its light.
determine the threshold voltage of an LED from a current–voltage graph.
determine the Planck constant from the slope of a line fitted to threshold voltages.
prior: The energy of a photon is $E = hf = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$ is the energy that an electron receives in a voltage of $1\,\text{V}$ (chapter *The photoelectric effect and the photon*)

When an electron moves from a higher energy level to a lower one, a photon is created whose energy is the difference of the energies of the levels (chapter *Spectra reveal the energy levels of atoms*)
The states and energies of the electrons of an atom are quantised (chapter *The wave-mechanical model of the atom and orbitals*)

activities.text: A red, a green and a blue LED are connected in parallel to the same adjustable voltage source, and the voltage is raised slowly from zero. The LEDs do not light up at the same time, although their voltage is the same at every moment.
activities.question: What decides the voltage at which an LED lights up, and how can the Planck constant be measured from this?

activities.title: Review: the energy of a photon
activities.prompt: The wavelength of red light is $630\,\text{nm}$ and that of blue light $470\,\text{nm}$. Which light has a photon of greater energy?

choices.text: Blue, because a shorter wavelength gives the photon greater energy.
choices.feedback: Correct. The energy of a photon is $E = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ (chapter *The photoelectric effect and the photon*). The energy of a photon of blue light is about $1240\,\text{eV}\,\text{nm} : 470\,\text{nm} \approx 2.64\,\text{eV}$ and that of red light about $1240\,\text{eV}\,\text{nm} : 630\,\text{nm} \approx 1.97\,\text{eV}$.

choices.text: Red, because a longer wave carries more energy with it.
choices.feedback: The energy of a photon is $E = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$: it *decreases* when the wavelength grows. The energy of a red photon is about $1.97\,\text{eV}$ and that of a blue one about $2.64\,\text{eV}$.

choices.text: Equal, because both photons travel at the same speed of light.
choices.feedback: The same speed does not mean the same energy. The energy of a photon depends on the frequency, $E = hf$, and the frequency of blue light, whose wavelength is shorter, is greater, so the energy of its photon is greater.

activities.title: Prediction 1: the same voltage, different colours
activities.prompt: Six LEDs of different colours, from red to violet, are connected in turn to the same voltage of $2.20\,\text{V}$. How do the currents through the LEDs differ from each other?

choices.text: The current through all of them is equal, because the voltage is the same and the LEDs are similar components.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the current through the red LED is $17.8\,\text{mA}$, through the green one only $0.11\,\text{mA}$, and practically no current flows through the blue and violet ones. An LED is not a resistor: a current flows through it only when the voltage is enough to give an electron the energy of a photon.

choices.text: The current of the red one is greatest and those of the blue and violet ones almost zero, because their photons require more energy.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: the current of the red LED is $17.8\,\text{mA}$, that of the orange one $13.9\,\text{mA}$, that of the yellow one $11.1\,\text{mA}$, that of the green one $0.11\,\text{mA}$, and the current of the blue and violet ones is practically zero. The voltage $2.20\,\text{V}$ gives an electron the energy $2.20\,\text{eV}$, which is enough to create a red photon, about $2.0\,\text{eV}$, but not a blue one, about $2.6\,\text{eV}$.

choices.text: The current of the blue and violet ones is greatest and that of the red one smallest, because photons of short-wavelength light have the most energy.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the current of the blue and violet LEDs is practically zero and that of the red one $17.8\,\text{mA}$. Precisely because the energy of a blue photon is large, about $2.6\,\text{eV}$, an electron needs a voltage greater than $2.20\,\text{V}$ to create it.

activities.title: Prediction 2: current as a function of voltage
activities.prompt: The voltage of a red LED is increased gradually from $1.50\,\text{V}$ to $2.40\,\text{V}$. How does the current through the LED change?

choices.text: The current grows steadily and in direct proportion to the voltage, starting from zero, as in a resistor.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: at the voltage $1.50\,\text{V}$ the current is practically zero, and even at $1.80\,\text{V}$ only $0.19\,\text{mA}$. Only above about $1.9\,\text{V}$ does the current grow, by about $5.6\,\text{mA}$ for every $0.10\,\text{V}$. An LED does not obey Ohm's law.

choices.text: The current is almost zero up to a certain voltage and then grows steeply and almost linearly.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: in the range $1.50$–$1.80\,\text{V}$ the current is less than $0.2\,\text{mA}$, but at $2.00\,\text{V}$ it is $6.7\,\text{mA}$ and at $2.40\,\text{V}$ $28.9\,\text{mA}$. Because of conservation of energy, an electron must receive at least approximately the energy of a photon before the LED can emit light.

choices.text: The current grows until the LED lights up and stays the same after that, even if the voltage is raised further.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: after the LED lights up the current still grows, from $6.7\,\text{mA}$ at $2.00\,\text{V}$ to $28.9\,\text{mA}$ at $2.40\,\text{V}$, and the LED becomes brighter. Each electron creates at most one photon, so a greater current means more photons.

activities.text: Choose an LED and adjust its voltage. Watch at what voltage the current starts to flow and the LED lights up. Every voltage you try leaves a point on the graph.
activities.howto: Choose an LED from the menu and adjust the voltage $U$ between the terminals of the LED with the slider. The ammeter ($\text{A}$) shows the current $I$ through the LED and the voltmeter ($\text{V}$) the voltage of the LED. The LED glows in its own colour, the brighter the greater the current, and the wavy lines are the photons it emits. On the right (on a phone, below) is the graph $(U, I)$: every voltage you try stays on it as a point in the colour of the LED, and the large point is the present state. *Clear the graph* removes the points. The graph does not show currents above $30\,\text{mA}$, and the readouts then show a warning.
activities.model: An adjustable voltage source and a protective resistor set the voltage of the LED; the slider shows the reading of the voltmeter directly. In the model the current is practically zero when the voltage is smaller than the threshold voltage of the LED, and above it grows linearly. For all the LEDs of the model the current grows equally steeply above the threshold voltage, which corresponds to a resistance of $18\,\Omega$. The threshold voltages of the model are slightly smaller than $\tfrac{hc}{e\lambda}$, as in real LEDs. The curve of a real LED is slightly curved also above the threshold voltage, and its threshold voltage changes a little with temperature. The readouts are values calculated by the model.
activities.calc: The current is calculated from the equation $I = \tfrac{s}{R} \ln\!\left(1 + \exp\tfrac{U - U_\text{k}}{s}\right)$, where $s = 0.035\,\text{V}$, $R = 18\,\Omega$ and $U_\text{k}$ is the threshold voltage of the LED. When $U$ is clearly greater than $U_\text{k}$, the equation is approximately $I = \tfrac{U - U_\text{k}}{R}$: a line that cuts the voltage axis at $U = U_\text{k}$. When $U$ is clearly smaller than $U_\text{k}$, the current is vanishingly small.

activities.title: Experiment 1: the same voltage, six LEDs
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. The voltage is locked at $2.20\,\text{V}$; change only the LED. Record the current for each of the six LEDs, at least three. Which LEDs light up, and what is their order?

activities.title: Experiment 2: the threshold voltage of a red LED
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. The red LED has been chosen; change only the voltage. Record the current at least at the voltages $1.50$; $1.70$; $1.80$; $1.90$; $2.00$; $2.10$; $2.20$; $2.30$ and $2.40\,\text{V}$. At what voltage does the current start to grow steeply?

question.prompt: Draw a graph $(U, I)$ of your measurements on paper or in Graphical Analysis Pro. Fit a line to the points where the current grows linearly (about $2.0$–$2.4\,\text{V}$) and extend it to the voltage axis. What is the threshold voltage of the red LED? Answer in volts.
hints: The threshold voltage is the voltage at which the extension of the straight part of the graph cuts the voltage axis, that is, the point $I = 0$.
On the straight part the current grows by about $5.6\,\text{mA}$ for every $0.10\,\text{V}$ added, so the slope is about $55\,\tfrac{\text{mA}}{\text{V}}$.

At the voltage $2.40\,\text{V}$ the current is $28.9\,\text{mA}$. According to the line, the current falls to zero when the voltage is reduced by $28.9\,\text{mA} : 55.5\,\tfrac{\text{mA}}{\text{V}}$.

mistakes.feedback: You read the voltage at which a current first starts to show. It depends on how small currents the meter can distinguish. The threshold voltage is obtained by extending the *straight part* of the graph to the voltage axis.

question.solution:
**Given:** the readings of the model for the red LED from the table: $2.00\,\text{V}$: $6.73\,\text{mA}$; $2.10\,\text{V}$: $12.23\,\text{mA}$; $2.20\,\text{V}$: $17.78\,\text{mA}$; $2.30\,\text{V}$: $23.33\,\text{mA}$; $2.40\,\text{V}$: $28.89\,\text{mA}$; at the voltages $1.90\,\text{V}$ and below the current is less than $2\,\text{mA}$

**Asked:** the threshold voltage $U_\text{k}$ in volts

**Principle:** Above the threshold voltage the current of the LED grows almost linearly. The threshold voltage is defined as the voltage at which the extension of this straight part cuts the voltage axis ($I = 0$). The points of the curved beginning do not belong to the line, so they are left out of the fit.

**Reading the graph:** The points in the range $2.00$–$2.40\,\text{V}$ are on a line, and the points below $1.90\,\text{V}$ curve towards zero. Two points far from each other are chosen from the line, $(2.10\,\text{V};\ 12.23\,\text{mA})$ and $(2.40\,\text{V};\ 28.89\,\text{mA})$.

**Formula:** the slope is $k = \dfrac{I_2 - I_1}{U_2 - U_1}$ and the line is $I = k\,(U - U_\text{k})$; at $I = I_2$ we get $U_\text{k} = U_2 - \dfrac{I_2}{k}$

**Conversions:** None are needed: the milliamperes cancel when the current is divided by the slope in the unit $\tfrac{\text{mA}}{\text{V}}$.

**Substitution:** $k = \dfrac{28.89\,\text{mA} - 12.23\,\text{mA}}{2.40\,\text{V} - 2.10\,\text{V}} = 55.53\,\tfrac{\text{mA}}{\text{V}}$, so $U_\text{k} = 2.40\,\text{V} - \dfrac{28.89\,\text{mA}}{55.53\,\text{mA/V}} = 2.40\,\text{V} - 0.520\,\text{V} = 1.880\,\text{V}$

**Answer:** $1.88\,\text{V}$, to a hundredth of a volt like the voltage readings.

**Reasonableness:** The energy of a photon of red light is $1240\,\text{eV}\,\text{nm} : 630\,\text{nm} \approx 1.97\,\text{eV}$, so the threshold voltage must be close to $1.97\,\text{V}$. The value obtained is about $0.1\,\text{V}$ smaller, as in real LEDs. In the table the current is also almost zero just below this voltage.

activities.title: Conclusion: what decides the lighting up?
activities.prompt: Write on the basis of your tables: in what order did the LEDs light up at the same voltage? How did the current of the red LED change as the voltage grew? Explain with the energy of a photon why an LED of a shorter wavelength needs a greater voltage.
activities.model: At the voltage $2.20\,\text{V}$ the current of the red LED was $17.8\,\text{mA}$, that of the orange one $13.9\,\text{mA}$, that of the yellow one $11.1\,\text{mA}$ and that of the green one only $0.11\,\text{mA}$; the blue and violet ones did not conduct at all. The shorter the wavelength, the greater the voltage that was needed. The current of the red LED was almost zero up to about $1.9\,\text{V}$ and then grew linearly, by about $5.6\,\text{mA}$ for every $0.10\,\text{V}$. The extension of the straight part cut the voltage axis at about $1.88\,\text{V}$: that is the threshold voltage of the red LED. Explanation: the voltage $U$ gives an electron the energy $eU$, and the electron creates a photon only when this energy is approximately the energy of the photon, $hf$. The energy of a photon of a shorter wavelength is greater, so the threshold voltage is also greater. The values are calculated by the model.
criteria: I stated that at the same voltage the red LED conducted the most and the blue and violet ones not at all, and I gave the numbers from the table.
I stated that the current was almost zero up to the threshold voltage and then grew almost linearly.
I stated how the threshold voltage is obtained from the extension of the straight part of the graph.
I explained that the energy $eU$ of the electron must be approximately the energy $hf$ of the photon, which is greater at a short wavelength.

activities.title: The Planck constant from the data of six LEDs
activities.text:
The table contains the threshold voltages of the six LEDs of the simulation. They have been determined in the same way as in experiment 2: for each LED the straight part of its graph $(U, I)$ has been extended to the voltage axis. If your school has a set of LEDs and measuring equipment, you can measure your own values and use them.

| LED | $\lambda$ (nm) | $U_\text{k}$ (V) |
|---|---|---|
| red | 630 | 1.88 |
| orange | 605 | 1.95 |
| yellow | 590 | 2.00 |
| green | 525 | 2.30 |
| blue | 470 | 2.52 |
| violet | 405 | 2.95 |

Process the data in Graphical Analysis Pro:

1. In the start window choose **Manual Entry** and type the columns $\lambda$ and $U_\text{k}$ with their units into the table.
2. Add the frequency column with the choice **New Calculated Column**. Write an expression that divides the speed of light $2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ by the wavelength in metres: remember that $1\,\text{nm} = 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$.
3. Choose $f$ for the horizontal axis of the graph and $U_\text{k}$ for the vertical axis.
4. Fit a line with the graph tools using the choices **Curve Fit**, **Linear** and **Apply**. The $m$ of the result box is the slope $k$; the program uses a decimal point.
activities.source_note: threshold voltages of the model of this chapter's simulation, not the results of a real measurement

question.prompt: Calculate the Planck constant from the slope of the fitted line. The elementary charge is $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. Answer in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$, for example in the form 6.5e-34.
hints: From the equation $eU_\text{k} = hf$ we get $U_\text{k} = \tfrac{h}{e}\,f$. Which quantity is the slope of the graph $(f, U_\text{k})$?
The slope is $k = \tfrac{h}{e}$, so $h = ek$. Check that the frequencies are of the order of $10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$.
The slope of the fit is about $4.05 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s}$. Multiply it by the elementary charge.

mistakes.feedback: This is the slope $k = \tfrac{h}{e}$ of the line in the unit $\text{V}\,\text{s}$. The Planck constant is obtained by multiplying it by the elementary charge: $h = ek$.

This is the slope $\tfrac{hc}{e}$ of the graph $(\tfrac{1}{\lambda}, U_\text{k})$ in the unit $\text{V}\,\text{m}$. Draw the graph as a function of the frequency $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$, or divide this slope by the speed of light and multiply by the elementary charge.

question.solution:
**Given:** from the table, the peak wavelengths of the six LEDs $405$–$630\,\text{nm}$ and the threshold voltages $1.88$–$2.95\,\text{V}$; $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$, $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$

**Asked:** the Planck constant $h$ in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$

**Principle:** At the threshold voltage the energy received by an electron is approximately the energy of a photon, $eU_\text{k} \approx hf$, so the points $(f, U_\text{k})$ are approximately on a line whose slope is $\tfrac{h}{e}$. The points are not exactly on the same line, so the line is fitted to all six points. An almost equal deviation for all the LEDs shifts the line but does not change the slope.

**Reading the graph:** The frequencies are $4.76$; $4.96$; $5.08$; $5.71$; $6.38$ and $7.40 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$. The linear fit gives the slope $m = 4.054 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\tfrac{\text{V}}{\text{Hz}}$ and the constant term $b = -0.050\,\text{V}$.

**Formula:** $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}$ and $k = \dfrac{h}{e}$, so $h = ek$

**Conversions:** wavelengths to metres, for example $630\,\text{nm} = 630 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$, whereby $f = \dfrac{2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}}{630 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 4.759 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$; the unit of the slope is $\tfrac{\text{V}}{\text{Hz}} = \text{V}\,\text{s}$

**Substitution:** $h = ek = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C} \cdot 4.054 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s} = 6.494 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$

**Answer:** $6.49 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, three significant figures like the threshold voltages.

**Reasonableness:** A check from the farthest points: $(2.95\,\text{V} - 1.88\,\text{V}) : (2.64 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}) \approx 4.05 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s}$, the same as in the fit. The result differs from the accepted value $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$ by about $-2.0\,\%$. The constant term $-0.05\,\text{V}$ is small compared with the threshold voltages, so the line passes almost through the origin, as the equation $eU_\text{k} = hf$ predicts.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the values of the model in the experiments and with the equation $eU_\text{k} \approx hf$. Then return to the question at the beginning: why does a blue LED need a higher voltage than a red one to light up?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A student writes in the lab report: "I fitted a line to the points $(f, U_\text{k})$. The line cuts the vertical axis at $-0.05\,\text{V}$ and does not pass through the origin. According to the equation $eU_\text{k} = hf$ the line should pass through the origin, so the measurement failed, and I cannot determine the Planck constant from the slope." Where is the error?

choices.text: An almost equal deviation for all the LEDs shifts the line but does not change the slope from which $h$ is obtained.
choices.feedback: Correct. The measured threshold voltage is slightly smaller than $\tfrac{hf}{e}$ for all the LEDs, by about $0.1\,\text{V}$. Such an almost constant difference shows in the constant term $b$, but the slope $\tfrac{h}{e}$ remains. This is why the Planck constant is determined precisely from the slope and not from one LED.

choices.text: The line must be forced to pass through the origin, whereby its slope gives the correct Planck constant.
choices.feedback: A line through the origin needs a physical justification, and the threshold voltages measured here are not exactly $\tfrac{hf}{e}$. If the line is forced to the origin, it turns according to the deviation of the points, and the slope is distorted. The slope of a freely fitted line is more reliable.

choices.text: The reasoning is correct: if the line does not pass through the origin, there is a gross error in the points, and the measurement must be repeated.
choices.feedback: A small constant term does not indicate a gross error. The threshold voltage is defined as the extension of the line, and the electrons also receive extra energy from thermal motion, so the measured value is slightly smaller than $\tfrac{hf}{e}$ for all the LEDs. This shifts the line but does not change the slope.

choices.text: The graph is wrong: the Planck constant is obtained only from a graph with the wavelength $\lambda$ on the horizontal axis.
choices.feedback: In the graph $(\lambda, U_\text{k})$ the points are not on a line, because $U_\text{k}$ is inversely proportional to the wavelength. A line is obtained when the frequency $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$ is on the horizontal axis, as the student has it. The error is in the conclusion drawn from the constant term.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: The remote control of a television has an LED whose light the eye cannot see. Its threshold voltage is measured to be $1.30\,\text{V}$. Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. Estimate the wavelength of the radiation of the LED. Answer in nanometres.
hints: At the threshold voltage the energy that an electron receives from the voltage source is approximately the energy of one photon.
Solve the wavelength $\lambda$ from the equation $eU_\text{k} = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.
$eU_\text{k} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C} \cdot 1.30\,\text{V} = 2.083 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$, so $\lambda = \tfrac{hc}{eU_\text{k}}$. Finally convert metres to nanometres.

mistakes.feedback: This is the wavelength in metres. Convert it to nanometres: $1\,\text{m} = 10^{9}\,\text{nm}$.
You left out the elementary charge. The voltage gives an electron the energy $eU_\text{k}$ in joules: $1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C} \cdot 1.30\,\text{V}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** threshold voltage $U_\text{k} = 1.30\,\text{V}$, $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$, $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$

**Asked:** the wavelength $\lambda$ of the radiation of the LED in nanometres

**Principle:** An LED starts to emit radiation when the energy $eU_\text{k}$ that an electron receives from the voltage source is approximately the energy $\tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ of one photon. The same principle applies to invisible infrared as to visible light. Because the measured threshold voltage is usually slightly smaller than $\tfrac{hf}{e}$, the result is an estimate.

**Formula:** $eU_\text{k} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{eU_\text{k}}$

**Conversions:** $eU_\text{k} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C} \cdot 1.30\,\text{V} = 2.0826 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$, because $1\,\text{C} \cdot 1\,\text{V} = 1\,\text{J}$; the result from metres to nanometres, $1\,\text{m} = 10^{9}\,\text{nm}$

**Substitution:** $hc = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s} \cdot 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s} = 1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m}}{2.0826 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 9.538 \cdot 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 954\,\text{nm}$

**Answer:** about $954\,\text{nm}$, three significant figures like the voltage $1.30\,\text{V}$.

**Reasonableness:** With round numbers $1240\,\text{V}\,\text{nm} : 1.30\,\text{V} \approx 950\,\text{nm}$. The wavelength is over $700\,\text{nm}$, so the radiation is infrared, which the eye cannot see, as the problem says. The real wavelength should be slightly shorter, because the measured threshold voltage is usually slightly smaller than $\tfrac{hf}{e}$: the LEDs of remote controls typically emit at a wavelength of about $940\,\text{nm}$.

activities.text: Practise on three levels. In the level 1 exercises one formula is used, in the level 2 exercises two steps are combined, such as the energy of a photon and the threshold voltage, and level 3 requires processing data or reasoning in a new situation.

activities.title: 1. A greater voltage
activities.prompt: A red LED shines at the voltage $2.2\,\text{V}$. What happens when its voltage is raised to $2.4\,\text{V}$?

choices.text: The LED shines brighter, but its light stays red.
choices.feedback: Correct. A greater voltage increases the current, so more photons are created in the LED every second. The energy of each photon is decided by the energy gap of the semiconductor, however, so the colour stays the same.

choices.text: The light becomes bluer, because the electrons receive more energy.
choices.feedback: The energy of a photon is approximately equal to the energy gap, and the energy gap does not change with the voltage. The extra energy turns into heat in the LED, and the colour stays red.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the LED has already lit up.
choices.feedback: Above the threshold voltage the current grows steeply with the voltage. A greater current means more photons per second, so the LED becomes brighter although the colour does not change.

activities.title: 2. The Planck constant from a graph
activities.prompt: The graph shows the threshold voltages of LEDs measured by another group as a function of frequency, and a line fitted to them. Read two points from the line and determine the Planck constant. The elementary charge is $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. Answer in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$.
hints: Choose two points far from each other on the line, where the line passes through the intersection of grid lines.
The slope is $k = \tfrac{\Delta U_\text{k}}{\Delta f}$, and the Planck constant is $h = ek$. Remember the factor $10^{14}$ of the frequency axis.
The line passes through the points $(4.6 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz};\ 1.80\,\text{V})$ and $(7.0 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz};\ 2.80\,\text{V})$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the slope $k = \tfrac{h}{e}$ of the line. Multiply it by the elementary charge: $h = ek$.
The numbers on the frequency axis are in the unit $10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$. Write the difference of the frequencies in hertz: $2.4 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** the fitted line of the graph and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$

**Asked:** the Planck constant $h$ in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$

**Principle:** At the threshold voltage $eU_\text{k} \approx hf$, so the slope of the graph $(f, U_\text{k})$ is $\tfrac{h}{e}$. The slope is read from the fitted line at two points far from each other, not from the measured points.

**Reading the graph:** The line passes through intersections of grid lines at $(4.6 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz};\ 1.80\,\text{V})$ and $(7.0 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz};\ 2.80\,\text{V})$. The spacing of the horizontal grid is $0.2 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$ and that of the vertical grid $0.1\,\text{V}$.

**Formula:** $k = \dfrac{U_2 - U_1}{f_2 - f_1} = \dfrac{h}{e}$, so $h = \dfrac{e\,(U_2 - U_1)}{f_2 - f_1}$

**Conversions:** The readings of the frequency axis in hertz: $4.6 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$ and $7.0 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$; $\text{C} \cdot \tfrac{\text{V}}{\text{Hz}} = \text{J}\,\text{s}$

**Substitution:** $U_2 - U_1 = 2.80\,\text{V} - 1.80\,\text{V} = 1.00\,\text{V}$ and $f_2 - f_1 = 7.0 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz} - 4.6 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz} = 2.4 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$, so $h = \dfrac{1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C} \cdot 1.00\,\text{V}}{2.4 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}} = 6.675 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$

**Answer:** $6.7 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, two significant figures, because the difference of the frequencies $2.4 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$ is read to two figures.

**Reasonableness:** The accepted value is $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, and the result differs from it by less than $1\,\%$. With the accepted value the line would rise by $1\,\text{V}$ over the frequency interval $\tfrac{e \cdot 1\,\text{V}}{h} = \tfrac{1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}}{6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}} = 2.42 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$, and in the graph the interval is $2.4 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$.

activities.title: 3. Explain: the blue and the red LED
activities.prompt: Explain with energy why a blue LED needs a greater voltage than a red one to light up. Mention in your explanation the electron, the energy gap and the photon.
criteria: I state that the voltage $U$ gives every electron the energy $eU$.
I state that the electron creates one photon when it falls across the energy gap, and the energy of the photon is approximately equal to the energy gap.
I justify that the energy of a photon of blue light is greater than that of red light, because its wavelength is shorter ($E = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$).
I conclude that the LED lights up when $eU_\text{k} \approx hf$, so the threshold voltage of the blue LED is greater.
activities.model: In an LED an electron falls from the conduction band into a hole of the valence band and creates one photon whose energy is approximately equal to the energy gap $E_\text{g}$ of the semiconductor. The voltage $U$ gives every electron that passes through the LED the energy $eU$, so photons can be created only when $eU$ is approximately the energy $hf$ of a photon. The wavelength of blue light is shorter than that of red light, so the energy $\tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ of its photon is greater: about $2.6\,\text{eV}$ instead of about $2.0\,\text{eV}$ for red. The energy gap of the semiconductor of a blue LED is therefore greater, and its threshold voltage is about $2.5\,\text{V}$, whereas that of a red one is about $1.9\,\text{V}$.
